openers.institutions-and-initiatives: Ideas need organizations to carry them into the world. The United Nations Environment Programme coordinates the UN's response to environmental problems, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature brings governments and conservation groups together. Researchers gather in the International Society for Ecological Economics and in the World Resources Institute, founded in 1982. Newer bodies, such as the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market and its Core Carbon Principles, try to set standards for carbon credits. This final chapter also looks at plans that help the poorest countries adapt to climate change, and at the toll climate change can take on people's minds.

reviews.institutions-and-initiatives: The institutions in this chapter grew out of the summits and ideas that came before them. UNEP was born at Stockholm in 1972, and IUCN's 1980 World Conservation Strategy was the first report with a chapter on sustainable development. Research bodies such as the International Society for Ecological Economics and the World Resources Institute supplied the measurements, from material flow accounts to satellite maps of forests. Newer efforts like the Core Carbon Principles and national adaptation plans show the same pattern at work today: rules and money meant to turn good intentions into results, and critics checking whether they do.

nature-hist-071.title: Robert Ayres and the metabolism of industry
nature-hist-071.text: Nothing is truly consumed. Robert Ayres (1932–2023), an American-born physicist and economist, applied the {{ref:nature-eecon-118}} to economics. The first law, he argued, makes 'consumption' a misleading word, because transforming materials unavoidably creates large amounts of waste, some of it toxic. He originated the idea of industrial metabolism, the study of how materials flow and change through an economy, also called {{ref:nature-eecon-008}}. He criticized growth models that leave out energy, as if output came from labor and capital alone. With Benjamin Warr he found that growth accounting improves once the efficiency of energy conversion is included. He is named among the figures of ecological economics.

nature-hist-078.title: Ecological Economics, the field's flagship journal
nature-hist-078.text: Ecological Economics is a peer-reviewed journal published by Elsevier for the {{ref:nature-hist-029}}. Robert Costanza founded it in 1989 as its first editor-in-chief. It aims to join the study of 'nature's household', ecosystems, with 'humanity's household', the economy. It publishes both mainstream neoclassical and heterodox work, a mix that has sparked lively debate among the society's members over what {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} should be.

nature-hist-043.title: Kenneth Boulding and Spaceship Earth
nature-hist-043.text: In 1966 Kenneth Boulding (1910–1993) wrote 'The Economics of the Coming Spaceship Earth'. The English-born American economist, educator and peace activist argued that the economy must fit itself to an ecological system with limited resources, the idea of {{ref:nature-eecon-127}}. He suggested treating Earth's ecosystem as a stock of assets. He stressed that economic behavior is embedded in a larger interconnected system, and promoted an evolutionary rather than equilibrium approach to economics.

nature-hist-061.title: Gifford Pinchot and the wise use of forests
nature-hist-061.text: In 1905 Gifford Pinchot (1865–1946) and Theodore Roosevelt persuaded Congress to create the United States Forest Service, and Pinchot became its first chief. The American forester and politician is a key figure of the {{ref:nature-hist-014}}. He promoted scientific forestry and the controlled, profitable use of forests for the greatest benefit to people. Conservation, in his 'wise use' view, secured long-term benefits for society. Joan Martinez Alier names him a leading voice of the 'gospel of eco-efficiency'.

nature-hist-053.title: Gretchen Daily and Nature's Services
nature-hist-053.text: Gretchen Daily, an American environmental scientist and tropical ecologist born in 1964, helped make nature's benefits count in real decisions. In 1997 she edited Nature's Services: Societal Dependence on Natural Ecosystems, a foundational framework for {{ref:nature-found-004}}s. It served as a model for regulation in several regions and was a catalyst for the UN's Millennium Ecosystem Assessment. Her original definition kept ecosystem goods and services apart, a distinction later work lumped together. In 2005 she co-founded the Natural Capital Project with The Nature Conservancy and WWF. Its free software, InVEST, is used in 185 countries to show nature's values in specific decisions. Her 2002 book with Katherine Ellison, The New Economy of Nature, gives cases where companies or governments profited from conservation.

nature-hist-074.title: William Baumol on why harm is hard to price
nature-hist-074.text: William Baumol (1922–2017), an American economist among the world's most influential, was instrumental in framing Pigou's work for modern economics in 1972. His research recognized the basic role of non-convexities in causing {{ref:nature-found-045}}. He also made a key criticism of the {{ref:nature-pol-088}}: the social cost of an {{ref:nature-found-031}} is extraordinarily difficult, almost impossible, to measure.

nature-hist-058.title: Dennis Meadows and the limits of growth
nature-hist-058.text: From 1970 to 1972 at MIT, Dennis Meadows, an American systems scientist born in 1942, directed the Club of Rome project behind {{ref:nature-eecon-154}}. The 1972 book used the World3 model to explore how exponential growth meets finite resources, rather than to make specific predictions. By the 2004 30-Year Update, the message had shifted from slowing growth to managing an orderly retreat back below Earth's limits. He received the Japan Prize in 2009.

nature-hist-057.title: David Pearce, who priced the environment
nature-hist-057.text: The environment is under-priced, argued David Pearce (1941–2005), and the benefits of its services can be calculated. The British pioneer of {{ref:nature-found-030}} at University College London set out techniques for valuing nature. His early work on {{ref:nature-val-001}}, pollution and resource depletion came before these ideas reached mainstream policy. He advised UK ministers, was a lead author for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, and criticized the assumptions behind discounting future goods.

nature-hist-042.title: Kate Raworth and doughnut economics
nature-hist-042.text: Kate Raworth, an English economist born in 1970, drew the economy as a doughnut. Her model, {{ref:nature-eecon-146}}, aims to give everyone basic needs such as food and education without pushing past {{ref:nature-eco-597}} or limiting future generations. She first set out the idea in a 2012 paper and expanded it in her 2017 book. She criticizes unlimited growth as destroying planetary resources while serving people poorly. She worked on the UN Human Development Report and spent over a decade at Oxfam.

nature-hist-081.title: Martin Weitzman and climate's fat tails
nature-hist-081.text: Martin Weitzman, an American economist at Harvard, studied {{ref:nature-hist-007}} and catastrophe. He added the risk of dramatic climate change to cost-benefit analysis to argue for immediate action. The economy-climate system, he argued, may have 'fat tails', rare but disastrous outcomes that standard models handle poorly. He also showed when price controls beat quantity controls under uncertainty. With Gernot Wagner he co-wrote Climate Shock (2015).

nature-hist-072.title: Serge Latouche, voice of degrowth
nature-hist-072.text: Serge Latouche, a French emeritus professor of economics born in 1940, is one of the best-known advocates of {{ref:nature-eecon-143}}. He denounces consumer society, economism and even the notion of sustainable development. In his manifesto Farewell to Growth he credited Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen as degrowth's main theoretical source. The same book proposes 'ecomunicipalism', local action meant to start a virtuous cycle of quiet economic contraction.

nature-hist-068.title: Milner Schaefer and the economics of fishing
nature-hist-068.text: Milner Baily Schaefer (1912–1970) was an American fisheries scientist at the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission. He published a model of fish stocks in balance with fishing, based on the Verhulst growth model, with a catch equation that bears his name. He extended it to an unregulated fishery, where fishing effort rises until no profit is left, the balance H. Scott Gordon called bionomic equilibrium. Together their work, the {{ref:nature-res-017}}, laid the basis of quantitative fisheries economics.

nature-hist-054.title: Allen Kneese: pollution inside the model
nature-hist-054.text: Allen V. Kneese (1930–2001), an American economist, built pollution into economic models and studied incentives for environmental improvement, making him a pioneer of {{ref:nature-found-030}}. He worked at Resources for the Future from 1961. He was the first president of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and a founding editor of its journal. In 1990 he shared the first Volvo Environment Prize with {{ref:nature-hist-041}}.

nature-hist-066.title: Karl-Göran Mäler and the Beijer Institute
nature-hist-066.text: In 1992 Karl-Göran Mäler (1939–2020) and Partha Dasgupta founded the Beijer Institute of Ecological Economics, which Mäler directed until 2006. The Swedish economist worked across economics and {{ref:nature-eecon-059}}. He was a professor at the Stockholm School of Economics from 1975 to 2002, and he and Dasgupta shared the Volvo Environment Prize in 2002.

nature-hist-055.title: AnnMari Jansson, bridge between ecology and economy
nature-hist-055.text: In 1982 AnnMari Jansson (1934–2007), a Swedish systems ecologist, and the economist Karl-Göran Mäler gathered ecologists and economists at Saltsjöbaden for a symposium on joining the two fields. Her ecological work drew on the models of Howard T. Odum. She helped found the {{ref:nature-hist-029}} in 1988 and edited its journal from 1989.

nature-hist-070.title: Richard Norgaard and coevolving societies
nature-hist-070.text: Richard B. Norgaard, born in 1943, is a professor emeritus at Berkeley and one of the founders of {{ref:nature-eecon-059}}. His research treats development as {{ref:nature-eecon-139}}, a process in which social and environmental systems change each other. A 1975 paper of his showed farmers who hired independent pest experts earned more and used half as much pesticide as those advised by agribusiness. He was president of the {{ref:nature-hist-029}} from 1998 to 2001.

nature-hist-065.title: Karl William Kapp and the true social costs
nature-hist-065.text: To Karl William Kapp (1910–1976), calling pollution an 'externality' was a misnomer, as if the harm sat outside the economy. The German-American economist's {{ref:nature-found-086}} offers the heterodox alternative to the neoclassical idea of {{ref:nature-found-084}}. It addresses urgent socio-ecological problems and proposes preventive policies based on the precautionary principle. His 1950 work counts among the European predecessors of ecological economics.

nature-hist-073.title: Serhiy Podolynsky: energy and labor in 1880
nature-hist-073.text: Serhiy Podolynsky (1850–1891), a Ukrainian socialist, physician and sociologist, tried to reconcile socialism with the second law of thermodynamics, drawing on Marx, Darwin and Sadi Carnot. In 1880 he proposed a theory of value based on {{ref:nature-eecon-095}}, which Marx and Engels read and critiqued. Human labor, he held, only changes natural objects. The resources available to people grow only as photosynthesis captures the Sun's energy.

nature-hist-079.title: The Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
nature-hist-079.text: The Journal of Environmental Economics and Management is generally regarded as the top journal in natural resource and {{ref:nature-found-030}}. It is peer-reviewed and published six times a year. Ralph d'Arge and Allen V. Kneese were its founding editors. It was the official journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists until 2014.

nature-hist-041.title: John Krutilla and the value of wilderness
nature-hist-041.text: John V. Krutilla (1922–2003) invented the concept of {{ref:nature-val-054}}, the value of wilderness or a species simply existing, in his essay {{ref:nature-hist-025}}. The American economist has been described as creating or stimulating most of the agenda of modern {{ref:nature-found-030}}. He worked at Resources for the Future until retiring in 1988, and in 1990 he shared the first Volvo Environment Prize with Allen V. Kneese.

nature-hist-047.title: Pavan Sukhdev, the banker who priced nature
nature-hist-047.text: Pavan Sukhdev, an Indian environmental economist born in 1960, spent 14 years at Deutsche Bank before turning to nature. He was Study Leader of {{ref:nature-hist-001}}, whose 2008 Interim Report showed the economic weight of losing nature's services and linked it to ethics, equity and poverty. He then headed UNEP's Green Economy Initiative, which argued that a {{ref:nature-eecon-140}} drives wealth, jobs and poverty reduction rather than burdening growth. He was president of WWF International from 2017 to 2021.

nature-hist-080.title: Martin Faustmann, father of forest economics
nature-hist-080.text: When should a forester cut a stand of trees? Martin Faustmann answered in 1849 with his analysis of the best rotation. This German forester is regarded as the father of forest economics. {{ref:nature-res-106}} is still widely used in natural resource valuation. After his 1848 examinations he became chief forester of Dudenhofen near Darmstadt and stayed there until his death.

nature-hist-031.title: UNEP: the UN's voice on the environment
nature-hist-031.text: The United Nations Environment Programme coordinates responses to environmental issues within the UN system. It was created in 1972 after the {{ref:nature-hist-002}} and is based in Nairobi, Kenya. Its mandate covers climate change, marine and land ecosystems, and green economic development. Maurice Strong was its first head. Under Mostafa Tolba it negotiated the 1987 Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer. Its expert group on biological diversity, begun in 1988, led to the draft Convention on Biological Diversity. It runs the Regional Seas Programme, set up in 1974, and administers the CITES secretariat. Its achievements include the 2017 Minamata Convention limiting toxic mercury. Its governing body, the UN Environment Assembly, has 193 members. Yet a 2020 UNEP report found that most global biodiversity efforts had failed to meet their goals.

nature-hist-030.title: IUCN and the Red List of Threatened Species
nature-hist-030.text: Since 1964 one organization has kept the world's list of species at risk. The International Union for Conservation of Nature was founded on 5 October 1948 in Fontainebleau, France. It brings governments and conservation groups together for {{ref:nature-eco-140}} and the sustainable use of natural resources. It began on the initiative of UNESCO and Julian Huxley. It produces the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, first published as the Red Data Book, and the Red List of Ecosystems. Its 1980 World Conservation Strategy was the first report with a chapter on sustainable development. Drafting it led IUCN to accept that conservation by banning people no longer worked. It advises the major biodiversity and climate conventions. Critics say it long favored removing people from protected areas and took a mainly Northern view.

nature-hist-029.title: The International Society for Ecological Economics
nature-hist-029.text: The human economy is part of a finite biosphere and should respect ecological limits. That is the founding belief of the International Society for Ecological Economics, the field's main scholarly society, founded in 1989 largely on the work of {{ref:nature-hist-040}}. Through education, research, policy and social action, it works toward an equitable and ecologically sustainable society. Robert Costanza was its first president and first editor of its monthly journal, Ecological Economics, launched with Elsevier in 1989. It holds regular conferences, and regional societies such as the Mesoamerican one are affiliated with it.

nature-hist-032.title: World Resources Institute: measuring the planet
nature-hist-032.text: The World Resources Institute, a global non-profit research organization founded in 1982, studies sustainable practices for business, finance and governance. Its work centers on food, forests, water, energy, cities and climate. With companies it developed the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, a common standard for measuring emissions. With Google Earth Engine it built Global Forest Watch, which maps forest change from satellite images. In 1990 Anil Agarwal criticized one of its emissions studies as environmental colonialism.

nature-hist-033.title: The Integrity Council and the quality of carbon credits
nature-hist-033.text: In an August 2024 test, around a third of carbon credits failed the benchmark. The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market, set up in 2021, is an independent body that publishes the {{ref:nature-hist-034}}, criteria for high-integrity credits in the {{ref:nature-mkt-083}}. It judges crediting programs and approves categories of credits that may carry a label. In 2024 it ruled several renewable energy methods ineligible over additionality concerns. Whether this works is debated. Critics such as Barbara Haya note that programs already used such ideas yet still over-credited.

nature-hist-037.title: How climate change affects the mind
nature-hist-037.text: Climate change can harm people's mental and emotional well-being, not only their bodies. Three pathways have been suggested: direct exposure to extreme weather, indirect effects such as lost income, and simple awareness of climate risk. Falling farm output and lost tourism bring financial stress, which can lead to depression. In US and Mexican data, suicide rates rose by 0.7% and 3.1% for a 1 °C rise in monthly temperature. Eco-anxiety, though, is very rarely severe enough to need clinical treatment.

nature-hist-035.title: National adaptation plans for the poorest countries
nature-hist-035.text: A National Adaptation Programme of Action, or NAPA, is a plan in which a least developed country tells the {{ref:nature-clim-053}} its most urgent needs for {{ref:nature-clim-002}}. Government ministries, usually helped by development agencies, assess the country's vulnerability and list adaptation projects in priority order, using existing information rather than new research. Submitting one unlocks money from the Least Developed Countries Fund, which had at least US$415 million, with US$177 million approved for 47 projects.

nature-hist-034.title: Core Carbon Principles: ten tests for a credit
nature-hist-034.text: How can a buyer tell a good carbon credit from a bad one? The Core Carbon Principles are the {{ref:nature-hist-033}}'s ten-part benchmark. They cover governance, tracking, transparency, independent checks, {{ref:nature-mkt-144}}, permanence, sound measurement, no double counting, social safeguards and contribution to net zero. The full set was published in January 2024. They answer a real difficulty: a credit's claimed impact depends on guessing what would have happened without it.
